name: Threshold frequency
statement: A photocathode has work function $2.28$ eV. Using $h = 4.14\times 10^{-15}$ eV$\cdot$s, what is its threshold frequency, in Hz?
solution: Emission begins when $hf_0 = \phi$. So $f_0 = 2.28/(4.14\times 10^{-15}) = 5.51\times 10^{14}$ Hz.

name: Momentum of a photon
statement: A photon has energy $2.48$ eV. Using $c = 3.00\times 10^8$ m/s and $1\ \text{eV} = 1.602\times 10^{-19}$ J, what is its momentum in kg$\cdot$m/s?
solution: For a photon $p = E/c$. Converting, $E = 2.48 \times 1.602\times 10^{-19} = 3.97\times 10^{-19}$ J, so $p = 3.97\times 10^{-19}/(3.00\times 10^8) = 1.32\times 10^{-27}$ kg$\cdot$m/s.

name: Photons from a HeNe laser
statement: A helium-neon laser emits $1.00$ mW at $632.8$ nm. How many photons does it emit per second? Use $hc = 1240$ eV$\cdot$nm and $1\ \text{eV} = 1.602\times 10^{-19}$ J.
solution: Each photon carries $1240/632.8 = 1.96$ eV $= 3.14\times 10^{-19}$ J. Dividing the power by that, $N = 1.00\times 10^{-3}/3.14\times 10^{-19} = 3.19\times 10^{15}$ per second.

name: Cutoff for a 2.50 eV metal
statement: A metal has work function $2.50$ eV. What is its photoelectric threshold wavelength, in nm? Use $hc = 1240$ eV$\cdot$nm.
solution: Threshold means $hc/\lambda_0 = \phi$, so $\lambda_0 = 1240/2.50 = 496$ nm. Orange or red light will not eject electrons from this surface.

name: Wavelength of a 1 eV photon
statement: What wavelength corresponds to a photon energy of exactly $1.00$ eV, in nm? Use $hc = 1240$ eV$\cdot$nm.
solution: From $E = hc/\lambda$, $\lambda = 1240/1.00 = 1240$ nm. This near-infrared wavelength is a useful benchmark to memorize.

name: Ultraviolet photon in joules
statement: A germicidal lamp emits at $200$ nm. What is the energy of one of its photons, in joules? Use $hc = 1240$ eV$\cdot$nm and $1\ \text{eV} = 1.602\times 10^{-19}$ J.
solution: The photon energy is $1240/200 = 6.20$ eV. Converting, $E = 6.20 \times 1.602\times 10^{-19} = 9.93\times 10^{-19}$ J.

name: Work function from two stopping potentials
statement: A photocathode gives a stopping potential of $1.40$ V at $400$ nm and $2.43$ V at $300$ nm. What is the work function of the surface, in eV? Use $hc = 1240$ eV$\cdot$nm.
solution: Einstein's relation gives $eV_s = hc/\lambda - \phi$. From the first point, $\phi = 3.10 - 1.40 = 1.70$ eV; the second gives $4.13 - 2.43 = 1.70$ eV, consistent.

name: Speed of the fastest photoelectron
statement: Photoelectrons emerge with maximum kinetic energy $1.50$ eV. Taking $m_e = 9.11\times 10^{-31}$ kg and $1\ \text{eV} = 1.602\times 10^{-19}$ J, what is their maximum speed, in m/s?
solution: At these energies the electron is non-relativistic, so $v = \sqrt{2K/m}$. With $K = 2.40\times 10^{-19}$ J, $v = \sqrt{2(2.40\times 10^{-19})/(9.11\times 10^{-31})} = 7.26\times 10^5$ m/s.

name: Radiation pressure on a mirror
statement: Sunlight of intensity $1000$ W/m$^2$ falls perpendicularly on a perfectly reflecting mirror. What is the radiation pressure, in Pa? Use $c = 3.00\times 10^8$ m/s.
solution: A reflected photon reverses its momentum, so the pressure is $2I/c$. That is $2(1000)/(3.00\times 10^8) = 6.67\times 10^{-6}$ Pa.

name: Force on a solar sail
statement: A perfectly absorbing sail of area $100$ m$^2$ faces sunlight of intensity $1000$ W/m$^2$. What force does the light exert on it, in N? Use $c = 3.00\times 10^8$ m/s.
solution: For full absorption the force is $F = IA/c$, since the sail absorbs momentum at rate $P/c$. Here $F = (1000)(100)/(3.00\times 10^8) = 3.33\times 10^{-4}$ N.

name: Compton shift at 90 degrees
statement: An X-ray photon scatters off a free electron through $90.0^\circ$. Taking the Compton wavelength $h/m_ec = 0.002426$ nm, by how much does its wavelength increase, in nm?
solution: The Compton formula is $\Delta\lambda = (h/m_ec)(1-\cos\theta)$. At $\theta = 90^\circ$, $\cos\theta = 0$, so $\Delta\lambda$ equals the Compton wavelength, $0.002426$ nm.

name: Backscattered X-ray
statement: An X-ray photon is backscattered ($\theta = 180^\circ$) by a free electron. Using $h/m_ec = 0.002426$ nm, what is the increase in its wavelength, in nm?
solution: With $\theta = 180^\circ$, $1 - \cos\theta = 2$, so $\Delta\lambda = 2(0.002426) = 0.004852$ nm. This is the largest shift possible.

name: Photocurrent and photon count
statement: A phototube carries a saturated photocurrent of $1.00$ $\mu$A. If every incident photon ejects one electron, how many photons strike the cathode per second? Use $e = 1.602\times 10^{-19}$ C.
solution: Saturation means every emitted electron is collected, so the rate is $N = I/e$. That gives $N = 1.00\times 10^{-6}/1.602\times 10^{-19} = 6.24\times 10^{12}$ per second.

name: Slope of the Millikan line
statement: A student plots stopping potential against light frequency and gets a straight line. Theory says the slope equals $h/e$. What numerical slope should the student expect, in V$\cdot$s? Use $h = 4.14\times 10^{-15}$ eV$\cdot$s.
solution: From $eV_s = hf - \phi$, the slope is $h/e$. Expressing $h$ in eV$\cdot$s already divides by $e$, so the slope is numerically $4.14\times 10^{-15}$ V$\cdot$s.

name: Cesium in visible light
statement: Cesium has the lowest work function of the common metals, $2.14$ eV. What is its threshold wavelength, in nm? Use $hc = 1240$ eV$\cdot$nm.
solution: Setting $hc/\lambda_0 = \phi$ gives $\lambda_0 = 1240/2.14 = 579$ nm. Cesium therefore responds to yellow light, which is why it is used in visible-light phototubes.

name: Photoelectrons bent by a magnetic field
statement: Photoelectrons of maximum kinetic energy $2.00$ eV enter a uniform magnetic field of $1.00\times 10^{-4}$ T perpendicular to their velocity. What is the radius of the largest circular path, in m? Use $m_e = 9.11\times 10^{-31}$ kg and $e = 1.602\times 10^{-19}$ C.
solution: The fastest electrons have $v = \sqrt{2K/m} = 8.39\times 10^5$ m/s. The cyclotron radius is $r = mv/(eB) = (9.11\times 10^{-31})(8.39\times 10^5)/[(1.602\times 10^{-19})(1.00\times 10^{-4})] = 0.0477$ m.

name: Photons needed to warm a target
statement: How many $532$ nm photons must be absorbed to deposit $1.00$ J of energy? Use $hc = 1240$ eV$\cdot$nm and $1\ \text{eV} = 1.602\times 10^{-19}$ J.
solution: Each photon carries $1240/532 = 2.331$ eV $= 3.734\times 10^{-19}$ J. Then $N = 1.00/3.734\times 10^{-19} = 2.68\times 10^{18}$ photons.

name: Shortest X-ray from a tube
statement: An X-ray tube is run at $30.0$ kV. What is the shortest wavelength in its bremsstrahlung spectrum, in nm? Use $hc = 1240$ eV$\cdot$nm.
solution: The photon carries at most the electron's full kinetic energy, $30.0$ keV. So $\lambda_{\min} = 1240\ \text{eV}\cdot\text{nm}/(3.00\times 10^4\ \text{eV}) = 0.0413$ nm.

name: Energy given to a Compton electron
statement: An X-ray of wavelength $0.0500$ nm scatters off a free electron at $60.0^\circ$. How much kinetic energy does the electron gain, in eV? Use $hc = 1240$ eV$\cdot$nm and $h/m_ec = 0.002426$ nm.
solution: The shift is $\Delta\lambda = 0.002426(1-\cos 60^\circ) = 0.001213$ nm, so $\lambda' = 0.051213$ nm. Energy conservation gives $K = hc/\lambda - hc/\lambda' = 24800 - 24213 = 587$ eV.

name: Recoil direction of the electron
statement: A $0.0711$ nm X-ray (molybdenum $K_\alpha$) Compton-scatters at $90.0^\circ$. The electron recoil angle satisfies $\tan\varphi = \big[(1+E/m_ec^2)\tan(\theta/2)\big]^{-1}$. At what angle from the incident direction does the electron recoil, in degrees? Use $hc = 1240$ eV$\cdot$nm and $m_ec^2 = 0.511$ MeV.
solution: The photon energy is $1240/0.0711 = 1.744\times 10^4$ eV, so $E/m_ec^2 = 0.03413$. With $\theta = 90^\circ$, $\tan(\theta/2) = 1$ and $\tan\varphi = 1/1.0341 = 0.967$. Hence $\varphi = 44.0^\circ$.

name: Levitating a mirror with light
statement: A perfectly reflecting mirror of mass $1.00$ mg is to be held up against gravity by a laser beam aimed straight up at it. What laser power is required, in W? Use $g = 9.80$ m/s$^2$ and $c = 3.00\times 10^8$ m/s.
solution: A reflected beam of power $P$ delivers force $2P/c$. Setting $2P/c = mg$ gives $P = mgc/2 = (1.00\times 10^{-6})(9.80)(3.00\times 10^8)/2 = 1.47\times 10^3$ W.

name: Intensity does not change the cutoff
statement: A cathode with work function $2.00$ eV is illuminated at $450$ nm, and the light intensity is then tripled. What is the stopping potential after the intensity change, in volts? Use $hc = 1240$ eV$\cdot$nm.
solution: Stopping potential depends only on photon energy, not intensity: more photons means more electrons, not faster ones. So $V_s = 1240/450 - 2.00 = 2.756 - 2.00 = 0.756$ V both before and after.

name: Two metals, one lamp
statement: Two photocathodes with work functions $2.20$ eV and $3.50$ eV are illuminated by the same monochromatic source. The stopping potentials differ by exactly $1.30$ V, and the lower-work-function cathode gives $1.10$ V. What is the wavelength of the light, in nm? Use $hc = 1240$ eV$\cdot$nm.
solution: The difference in stopping potentials equals the difference in work functions, which is consistent here and gives no new information. Use one cathode: $hc/\lambda = \phi + eV_s = 2.20 + 1.10 = 3.30$ eV, so $\lambda = 1240/3.30 = 376$ nm.

name: Recoil of an emitting atom
statement: A sodium atom of mass $3.82\times 10^{-26}$ kg at rest emits a $589$ nm photon. What recoil speed does the atom acquire, in m/s? Use $h = 6.63\times 10^{-34}$ J$\cdot$s.
solution: Momentum conservation gives $mv = h/\lambda$. So $v = (6.63\times 10^{-34})/[(589\times 10^{-9})(3.82\times 10^{-26})] = 0.0295$ m/s. This tiny recoil is the basis of laser cooling.

name: Maximum energy loss of a gamma ray
statement: A $511$ keV annihilation photon backscatters off a free electron. How much kinetic energy does the electron receive, in keV? Use $hc = 1240$ eV$\cdot$nm and $h/m_ec = 0.002426$ nm.
solution: The photon's wavelength is $1240/511000 = 0.0024266$ nm, and backscattering adds $2(0.002426) = 0.004852$ nm, giving $\lambda' = 0.0072796$ nm. The scattered photon carries $1240/0.0072796 = 170$ keV, so the electron takes $511 - 170 = 341$ keV. This is the Compton edge.

name: Charging an isolated sphere with UV
statement: An isolated metal sphere of radius $2.00$ cm and work function $3.00$ eV is illuminated with $250$ nm light in vacuum. It charges positively until no more electrons can escape. How many electrons have left the sphere? Use $hc = 1240$ eV$\cdot$nm, $k = 8.99\times 10^9$ N$\cdot$m$^2$/C$^2$, $e = 1.602\times 10^{-19}$ C.
solution: Emission stops when the sphere's potential equals the maximum kinetic energy per unit charge: $V = 1240/250 - 3.00 = 1.96$ V. Then $Q = rV/k = (0.0200)(1.96)/(8.99\times 10^9) = 4.36\times 10^{-12}$ C, so $N = Q/e = 2.72\times 10^7$ electrons.

name: Energy of the n = 2 level
statement: Hydrogen levels are given by $E_n = -13.6\ \text{eV}/n^2$. What is the energy of the $n = 2$ level, in eV?

name: Ionization energy of hydrogen
statement: How much energy is needed to remove the electron from a ground-state hydrogen atom, in eV?
solution: Ionization takes the electron from $E_1 = -13.6$ eV to $E = 0$ at rest far away. The required energy is $13.6$ eV.

name: H-alpha wavelength
statement: A hydrogen atom drops from $n = 3$ to $n = 2$. What is the wavelength of the emitted photon, in nm? Use $hc = 1240$ eV$\cdot$nm.
solution: The energy released is $13.6(1/4 - 1/9) = 1.889$ eV. Then $\lambda = 1240/1.889 = 656$ nm, the red H-alpha line.

name: Radius of the third orbit
statement: The Bohr radius is $a_0 = 0.0529$ nm and $r_n = n^2 a_0$. What is the radius of the $n = 3$ orbit in hydrogen, in nm?

name: Ground state of singly ionized helium
statement: For a hydrogen-like ion, $E_n = -13.6\,Z^2/n^2$ eV. What is the ground-state energy of He$^+$ ($Z = 2$), in eV?

name: Lyman-alpha photon
statement: A hydrogen atom falls from $n = 2$ to $n = 1$. What is the wavelength of the emitted photon, in nm? Use $hc = 1240$ eV$\cdot$nm.
solution: The transition energy is $13.6(1 - 1/4) = 10.2$ eV, so $\lambda = 1240/10.2 = 122$ nm. This ultraviolet line is Lyman-alpha.

name: Quantized angular momentum
statement: Bohr's postulate is $L = n\hbar$ with $\hbar = 1.055\times 10^{-34}$ J$\cdot$s. What is the orbital angular momentum of an electron in the $n = 4$ orbit, in J$\cdot$s?
solution: Directly, $L = 4\hbar = 4(1.055\times 10^{-34}) = 4.22\times 10^{-34}$ J$\cdot$s.

name: Balmer series limit
statement: What is the shortest wavelength in the Balmer series of hydrogen, in nm? Use $hc = 1240$ eV$\cdot$nm.
solution: The series limit corresponds to $n = \infty \to 2$, an energy of $13.6/4 = 3.40$ eV. Then $\lambda = 1240/3.40 = 365$ nm.

name: Doubly ionized lithium
statement: What is the energy of the $n = 2$ level of Li$^{2+}$ ($Z = 3$), in eV?

name: Exciting from the ground state
statement: How much energy must a ground-state hydrogen atom absorb to reach the $n = 3$ level, in eV?

name: Orbital speed in the ground state
statement: In the Bohr model the orbital speed is $v_n = \alpha c/n$ with the fine-structure constant $\alpha = 1/137$. Using $c = 3.00\times 10^8$ m/s, what is the electron's speed in the $n = 1$ orbit of hydrogen, in m/s?
solution: For $n = 1$, $v = \alpha c = (3.00\times 10^8)/137 = 2.19\times 10^6$ m/s. That is under 1% of $c$, which justifies the non-relativistic treatment.

name: H-gamma line
statement: What is the wavelength of the $n = 5 \to 2$ transition in hydrogen, in nm? Use $hc = 1240$ eV$\cdot$nm.
solution: The photon energy is $13.6(1/4 - 1/25) = 2.856$ eV, so $\lambda = 1240/2.856 = 434$ nm, the blue-violet H-gamma line.

name: Which level does the atom reach?
statement: A ground-state hydrogen atom absorbs a photon of exactly $12.75$ eV. What is the principal quantum number of the level it reaches?
solution: Solve $13.6(1 - 1/n^2) = 12.75$, giving $1/n^2 = 0.0625$ and $n^2 = 16$. The atom lands in $n = 4$.

name: Counting spectral lines
statement: A sample of hydrogen atoms is excited to the $n = 4$ level. How many distinct spectral lines can appear as the atoms cascade down?
solution: Every pair of levels from $1$ to $4$ gives one line, so the count is $\binom{4}{2} = 6$: the transitions $4\to3, 4\to2, 4\to1, 3\to2, 3\to1, 2\to1$.

name: Frequency of the electron's orbit
statement: In the $n = 1$ Bohr orbit the electron moves at $2.19\times 10^6$ m/s on a circle of radius $5.29\times 10^{-11}$ m. How many revolutions does it make per second?
solution: The orbital frequency is $f = v/(2\pi r) = (2.19\times 10^6)/[2\pi(5.29\times 10^{-11})] = 6.59\times 10^{15}$ Hz.

name: Franck-Hertz photons from mercury
statement: In a Franck-Hertz tube, mercury vapor shows current dips every $4.90$ V. What is the wavelength of the light emitted when the excited mercury atoms decay, in nm? Use $hc = 1240$ eV$\cdot$nm.
solution: Each dip means electrons lost $4.90$ eV exciting a mercury atom, so the excited state lies $4.90$ eV above the ground state. The emitted photon has $\lambda = 1240/4.90 = 253$ nm, in the ultraviolet.

name: Potential energy in the ground state
statement: A ground-state hydrogen atom has total energy $-13.6$ eV. Using the virial theorem for a Coulomb potential, what is the electron's potential energy, in eV?
solution: For an inverse-square force the virial theorem gives $\langle U\rangle = 2E$ and $\langle K\rangle = -E$. Hence $U = 2(-13.6) = -27.2$ eV, with $K = +13.6$ eV.

name: Muonic hydrogen
statement: A muon ($207$ times the electron mass) replaces the electron in a hydrogen atom. Treating the proton as infinitely heavy, what is the ground-state binding energy of muonic hydrogen, in keV?
solution: Bohr energies scale linearly with the orbiting particle's mass, $E_1 \propto m$. So $E_1 = 207 \times 13.6\ \text{eV} = 2.82\times 10^3$ eV $= 2.82$ keV, and the orbit shrinks by the same factor of $207$.

name: Positronium ground state
statement: Positronium is a bound electron-positron pair. Using the reduced mass, what is the magnitude of its ground-state binding energy, in eV?
solution: For equal masses the reduced mass is $\mu = m_e/2$, and Bohr energies scale with $\mu$. So the binding energy is $13.6/2 = 6.80$ eV.

name: Identifying an absorption line
statement: A stellar spectrum shows hydrogen absorption at $486$ nm out of the $n = 2$ level. What is the upper principal quantum number of the transition? Use $hc = 1240$ eV$\cdot$nm.

name: Paschen series longest line
statement: What is the longest wavelength in the Paschen series (transitions ending on $n = 3$) of hydrogen, in nm? Use $hc = 1240$ eV$\cdot$nm.
solution: The longest wavelength comes from the smallest gap, $n = 4 \to 3$: $13.6(1/9 - 1/16) = 0.661$ eV. So $\lambda = 1240/0.661 = 1.88\times 10^3$ nm, in the infrared.

name: Rydberg constant from the model
statement: The Rydberg formula is $1/\lambda = R(1/n_f^2 - 1/n_i^2)$. Using $13.6$ eV for the Rydberg energy and $hc = 1240$ eV$\cdot$nm, what is $R$ in m$^{-1}$?
solution: Comparing $hc/\lambda = 13.6(1/n_f^2 - 1/n_i^2)$ with the Rydberg formula gives $R = 13.6/hc$. Numerically $R = 13.6/1240\ \text{nm}^{-1} = 0.01097\ \text{nm}^{-1} = 1.10\times 10^7$ m$^{-1}$.

name: He+ line matching H-alpha
statement: A He$^+$ ion ($Z = 2$) emits a photon of exactly the same wavelength as hydrogen's $n = 3 \to 2$ line. The transition ends on $n_f = 4$. What is the upper level $n_i$?
solution: Hydrogen's H-alpha energy is $13.6(1/4 - 1/9) = 1.889$ eV. For He$^+$, $4(13.6)(1/16 - 1/n_i^2) = 1.889$ gives $1/n_i^2 = 0.02778$, so $n_i = 6$. The $Z = 2$ spectrum reproduces the hydrogen lines whenever both quantum numbers are doubled.

name: Recoil energy on emission
statement: A hydrogen atom at rest emits a $10.2$ eV Lyman-alpha photon. Taking the atomic rest energy as $938$ MeV, how much kinetic energy does the recoiling atom carry, in eV?
solution: Momentum conservation gives the atom $p = E_\gamma/c$, so $K = p^2/2M = E_\gamma^2/(2Mc^2)$. That is $(10.2)^2/(2\times 9.383\times 10^8) = 5.54\times 10^{-8}$ eV, utterly negligible compared with the line energy.

name: Magnetic field at the proton
statement: Treat the $n = 1$ electron as a point charge circling at $2.19\times 10^6$ m/s at radius $5.29\times 10^{-11}$ m. What magnetic field does it produce at the nucleus, in T? Use $\mu_0/4\pi = 1.00\times 10^{-7}$ T$\cdot$m/A and $e = 1.602\times 10^{-19}$ C.
solution: The Biot-Savart field of a moving point charge at the center of its orbit is $B = (\mu_0/4\pi)\,ev/r^2$. So $B = 10^{-7}(1.602\times 10^{-19})(2.19\times 10^6)/(5.29\times 10^{-11})^2 = 12.5$ T.

name: Threshold for collisional excitation
statement: A ground-state hydrogen atom moving freely strikes a second ground-state hydrogen atom at rest. What is the minimum kinetic energy of the incoming atom that can excite one atom to $n = 2$, in eV?
solution: Momentum must be conserved, so the two equal-mass atoms cannot both stop; at threshold they move together with half the initial speed, retaining half the kinetic energy. Only half the incoming energy is available for excitation, so $K_{\min} = 2 \times 10.2 = 20.4$ eV.

name: Deuterium isotope shift
statement: Hydrogen's H-alpha line sits at $656.47$ nm. Deuterium's nucleus is heavier, with $m_e/m_d = 1/3670.5$ versus $m_e/m_p = 1/1836.15$. What is the wavelength shift $\lambda_H - \lambda_D$, in nm?
solution: Level energies scale with the reduced mass $\mu = m_e/(1 + m_e/M)$, so $\lambda \propto 1/\mu$ and $\lambda_D/\lambda_H = \mu_H/\mu_D = (1+1/3670.5)^{-1}(1+1/1836.15)$. This gives $\lambda_D = 656.29$ nm and a shift of $0.179$ nm, which is how deuterium was discovered.

name: Do Balmer and Paschen overlap?
statement: The Balmer series runs from $365$ nm to $656$ nm. What is the shortest wavelength of the Paschen series, in nm? Use $hc = 1240$ eV$\cdot$nm.
solution: The Paschen series limit is $n = \infty \to 3$, with energy $13.6/9 = 1.511$ eV. Then $\lambda = 1240/1.511 = 820$ nm, so the Paschen series lies entirely beyond the Balmer series and the two do not overlap.

name: A Rydberg atom
statement: A hydrogen atom is prepared in the $n = 100$ level. What is the wavelength of the photon emitted in the $n = 100 \to 99$ transition, in cm? Use $hc = 1240$ eV$\cdot$nm.
solution: The energy gap is $13.6(1/99^2 - 1/100^2) = 2.761\times 10^{-5}$ eV. Then $\lambda = 1240/2.761\times 10^{-5} = 4.49\times 10^7$ nm $= 4.49$ cm, a microwave photon. Such transitions are how Rydberg atoms are detected.

name: A gravitationally bound atom
statement: Suppose an electron and a proton were bound only by gravity. Repeating the Bohr derivation with $Gm_em_p$ in place of $ke^2$ gives $r_1 = \hbar^2/(Gm_e^2m_p)$. Evaluate this radius, in meters. Use $\hbar = 1.055\times 10^{-34}$ J$\cdot$s, $G = 6.674\times 10^{-11}$, $m_e = 9.109\times 10^{-31}$ kg, $m_p = 1.673\times 10^{-27}$ kg.
solution: Substituting, the numerator is $\hbar^2 = 1.112\times 10^{-68}$ and the denominator is $Gm_e^2m_p = 9.26\times 10^{-98}$. The ratio is $1.20\times 10^{29}$ m, roughly $10^{13}$ light years, which shows just how weak gravity is compared with the Coulomb force.

name: Wavelength of a slow electron
statement: An electron moves at $1.00\times 10^6$ m/s. What is its de Broglie wavelength, in m? Use $h = 6.63\times 10^{-34}$ J$\cdot$s and $m_e = 9.11\times 10^{-31}$ kg.
solution: The de Broglie relation is $\lambda = h/p = h/(mv)$. So $\lambda = 6.63\times 10^{-34}/[(9.11\times 10^{-31})(1.00\times 10^6)] = 7.28\times 10^{-10}$ m.

name: Wavelength of a baseball
statement: A $0.145$ kg baseball is thrown at $40.0$ m/s. What is its de Broglie wavelength, in m? Use $h = 6.63\times 10^{-34}$ J$\cdot$s.
solution: $\lambda = h/(mv) = 6.63\times 10^{-34}/(0.145 \times 40.0) = 1.14\times 10^{-34}$ m. This is unimaginably smaller than any aperture, which is why baseballs never diffract.

name: Electron accelerated through 100 V
statement: A non-relativistic electron accelerated through $V$ volts has $\lambda = 1.226/\sqrt{V}$ nm. What is the wavelength of an electron accelerated through $100$ V, in nm?
solution: Substituting $V = 100$: $\lambda = 1.226/10.0 = 0.1226$ nm. That is comparable to atomic spacings, which is why such electrons diffract from crystals.

name: Proton versus electron at equal speed
statement: A proton and an electron move at the same speed. Taking $m_p/m_e = 1836$, what is the ratio of the proton's de Broglie wavelength to the electron's?
solution: At equal speeds $\lambda \propto 1/m$, so $\lambda_p/\lambda_e = m_e/m_p = 1/1836 = 5.45\times 10^{-4}$.

name: Momentum from a wavelength
statement: A particle has momentum $2.00\times 10^{-24}$ kg$\cdot$m/s. What is its de Broglie wavelength, in m? Use $h = 6.63\times 10^{-34}$ J$\cdot$s.

name: Electron in a 0.10 nm box
statement: An electron is confined to a one-dimensional box of length $0.100$ nm. Using $E_n = n^2(hc)^2/(8\,m_ec^2\,L^2)$ with $hc = 1240$ eV$\cdot$nm and $m_ec^2 = 511000$ eV, what is the ground-state energy, in eV?

name: Minimum momentum uncertainty
statement: An electron's position is known to within $1.00\times 10^{-10}$ m. What is the minimum uncertainty in its momentum, in kg$\cdot$m/s? Use $\Delta x\,\Delta p \ge \hbar/2$ with $\hbar = 1.055\times 10^{-34}$ J$\cdot$s.
solution: Rearranging, $\Delta p \ge \hbar/(2\Delta x) = 1.055\times 10^{-34}/(2\times 10^{-10}) = 5.28\times 10^{-25}$ kg$\cdot$m/s.

name: Thermal neutron wavelength
statement: A neutron is in thermal equilibrium at $300$ K, so its rms momentum is $\sqrt{3mk_BT}$. What is its de Broglie wavelength, in m? Use $h = 6.63\times 10^{-34}$ J$\cdot$s, $m_n = 1.675\times 10^{-27}$ kg, $k_B = 1.381\times 10^{-23}$ J/K.
solution: The rms momentum is $\sqrt{3(1.675\times 10^{-27})(1.381\times 10^{-23})(300)} = 4.56\times 10^{-24}$ kg$\cdot$m/s. Then $\lambda = h/p = 1.45\times 10^{-10}$ m, roughly an atomic spacing, which is why reactor neutrons make good crystal probes.

name: A one-electron-volt electron
statement: Using $\lambda = 1.226/\sqrt{V}$ nm, what is the de Broglie wavelength of an electron with $1.00$ eV of kinetic energy, in nm?
solution: With $V = 1.00$ V, $\lambda = 1.226/1.00 = 1.226$ nm. Note this is far shorter than a $1$ eV photon's wavelength of $1240$ nm.

name: Compton wavelength of the electron
statement: The Compton wavelength is $h/(m_ec) = hc/(m_ec^2)$. Using $hc = 1240$ eV$\cdot$nm and $m_ec^2 = 0.511$ MeV, what is it, in pm?
solution: $\lambda_C = 1240\ \text{eV}\cdot\text{nm}/(5.11\times 10^5\ \text{eV}) = 2.43\times 10^{-3}$ nm $= 2.43$ pm.

name: Davisson-Germer angle
statement: In the Davisson-Germer experiment, $54$ V electrons scatter from a nickel surface whose atomic rows are spaced $0.215$ nm apart. The first-order surface-grating maximum satisfies $d\sin\theta = \lambda$. At what angle does it appear, in degrees? Use $\lambda = 1.226/\sqrt{V}$ nm.
solution: The electron wavelength is $1.226/\sqrt{54} = 0.1668$ nm. Then $\sin\theta = 0.1668/0.215 = 0.776$ and $\theta = 50.9^\circ$, matching the observed peak that confirmed matter waves.

name: Electron microscope wavelength
statement: A transmission electron microscope accelerates electrons through $100$ kV. Using the non-relativistic formula $\lambda = 1.226/\sqrt{V}$ nm, what wavelength does this predict, in pm?
solution: $\lambda = 1.226/\sqrt{1.00\times 10^5} = 3.88\times 10^{-3}$ nm $= 3.88$ pm. The true relativistic value is about 5% smaller, but either way the resolution far exceeds any light microscope.

name: Transition in a quantum well
statement: An electron sits in a $0.500$ nm one-dimensional box. How much energy is released when it drops from $n = 2$ to $n = 1$, in eV? Use $hc = 1240$ eV$\cdot$nm and $m_ec^2 = 511000$ eV.

name: Neutron for crystallography
statement: A neutron has kinetic energy $0.0250$ eV. What is its de Broglie wavelength, in nm? Use $\lambda = hc/\sqrt{2mc^2K}$ with $hc = 1240$ eV$\cdot$nm and $m_nc^2 = 939.6$ MeV.

name: Electron with an optical wavelength
statement: How fast must an electron move for its de Broglie wavelength to equal $500$ nm, the wavelength of green light? Give the speed in m/s. Use $h = 6.63\times 10^{-34}$ J$\cdot$s and $m_e = 9.11\times 10^{-31}$ kg.
solution: From $\lambda = h/(mv)$, $v = h/(m\lambda) = 6.63\times 10^{-34}/[(9.11\times 10^{-31})(5.00\times 10^{-7})] = 1.46\times 10^3$ m/s. A very slow electron indeed.

name: Equal kinetic energies
statement: A proton and an electron have the same non-relativistic kinetic energy. Taking $m_p/m_e = 1836$, what is the ratio $\lambda_e/\lambda_p$?
solution: At fixed $K$, $p = \sqrt{2mK}$, so $\lambda \propto 1/\sqrt{m}$. The ratio is $\sqrt{m_p/m_e} = \sqrt{1836} = 42.8$.

name: Standing wave around a Bohr orbit
statement: De Broglie explained Bohr quantization by requiring $2\pi r_n = n\lambda$. For hydrogen's $n = 3$ orbit, $r_3 = 0.476$ nm. What is the electron's wavelength there, in nm?
solution: Three full wavelengths must fit around the circumference: $\lambda = 2\pi r_3/3 = 2\pi(0.476)/3 = 0.997$ nm. This standing-wave condition is exactly equivalent to $L = n\hbar$.

name: Alpha particle in an accelerator
statement: An alpha particle (charge $2e$, rest energy $3727$ MeV) is accelerated through $1.00$ MV. What is its de Broglie wavelength, in m? Use $\lambda = hc/\sqrt{2mc^2K}$ and $hc = 1240$ eV$\cdot$nm.
solution: Its charge is $2e$, so $K = 2.00$ MeV. Then $\sqrt{2(3.727\times 10^9)(2.00\times 10^6)} = 1.221\times 10^8$ eV and $\lambda = 1240/1.221\times 10^8 = 1.02\times 10^{-5}$ nm $= 1.02\times 10^{-14}$ m.

name: Why electrons are not in the nucleus
statement: Suppose an electron were confined inside a nucleus of size $1.00\times 10^{-14}$ m. Estimate its momentum from $\Delta p \approx \hbar/\Delta x$ and give $pc$ in MeV. Use $\hbar c = 197.3$ eV$\cdot$nm.
solution: Here $\Delta x = 1.00\times 10^{-5}$ nm, so $pc \approx \hbar c/\Delta x = 197.3/1.00\times 10^{-5} = 1.97\times 10^7$ eV $= 19.7$ MeV. That vastly exceeds nuclear binding energies per nucleon, so electrons cannot be nuclear constituents.

name: Cold helium atoms
statement: Helium atoms (mass $4.00$ u, $1\ \text{u} = 1.6605\times 10^{-27}$ kg) are cooled to $4.00$ K. Using rms momentum $\sqrt{3mk_BT}$, what is their de Broglie wavelength, in m? Use $h = 6.63\times 10^{-34}$ J$\cdot$s and $k_B = 1.381\times 10^{-23}$ J/K.
solution: The mass is $6.64\times 10^{-27}$ kg, and $p = \sqrt{3mk_BT} = 1.049\times 10^{-24}$ kg$\cdot$m/s. Then $\lambda = h/p = 6.32\times 10^{-10}$ m, already comparable to atomic spacings.

name: Wavelength of a photon and an electron
statement: A photon and an electron both have de Broglie wavelength $0.100$ nm. What is the ratio of the photon's energy to the electron's kinetic energy? Use $hc = 1240$ eV$\cdot$nm and $m_ec^2 = 511000$ eV.
solution: Equal wavelengths mean equal momenta, but the two relate energy to momentum differently. The photon has $E = pc = 1240/0.100 = 12400$ eV, while the non-relativistic electron has $K = (pc)^2/(2m_ec^2) = 1.538\times 10^8/1.022\times 10^6 = 150.5$ eV. The ratio is $12400/150.5 = 82.4$.

name: Slit width for electron diffraction
statement: Electrons accelerated through $10.0$ kV pass through a single slit and the first diffraction minimum appears at $1.00\times 10^{-3}$ rad. What is the slit width, in nm? Use $\lambda = 1.226/\sqrt{V}$ nm.
solution: The electron wavelength is $1.226/\sqrt{10^4} = 0.01226$ nm. With $a\sin\theta = \lambda$ and small $\theta$, $a = 0.01226/1.00\times 10^{-3} = 12.3$ nm.

name: Relativistic electron wavelength
statement: An electron has kinetic energy $1.00$ MeV. What is its de Broglie wavelength, in pm? Use $hc = 1240$ eV$\cdot$nm and $m_ec^2 = 0.511$ MeV.
solution: At this energy the non-relativistic formula fails. Total energy is $E = 1.511$ MeV, so $pc = \sqrt{E^2 - (m_ec^2)^2} = \sqrt{2.283 - 0.261} = 1.422$ MeV. Then $\lambda = hc/pc = 1240/1.422\times 10^6 = 8.72\times 10^{-4}$ nm $= 0.872$ pm.

name: Electron double slit
statement: A beam of $50.0$ keV electrons passes through two slits $1.00$ $\mu$m apart, with a detector $1.00$ m away. What is the spacing between adjacent interference fringes, in $\mu$m? Use $\lambda = 1.226/\sqrt{V}$ nm.
solution: The wavelength is $1.226/\sqrt{5.00\times 10^4} = 5.48\times 10^{-3}$ nm $= 5.48\times 10^{-12}$ m. The fringe spacing is $\lambda L/d = (5.48\times 10^{-12})(1.00)/(1.00\times 10^{-6}) = 5.48$ $\mu$m.

name: Nucleon confined in a nucleus
statement: Model a proton as confined to a one-dimensional box of length $5.00$ fm. What is its ground-state energy, in MeV? Use $E_1 = (hc)^2/(8\,m_pc^2L^2)$, $hc = 1240$ eV$\cdot$nm, $m_pc^2 = 938.3$ MeV.
solution: Convert $L = 5.00\times 10^{-6}$ nm. Then $E_1 = (1240)^2/[8(9.383\times 10^8)(2.50\times 10^{-11})] = 1.5376\times 10^6/0.1877 = 8.19\times 10^6$ eV $= 8.19$ MeV, the right order of magnitude for nuclear energies.

name: Uncertainty estimate of the hydrogen atom
statement: Estimate the hydrogen ground state by writing $E(r) = \hbar^2/(2m_er^2) - ke^2/r$, using $p \approx \hbar/r$, and minimizing over $r$. What minimum energy does this give, in eV? (The Rydberg energy is $13.6$ eV.)
solution: Setting $dE/dr = 0$ gives $-\hbar^2/(m_er^3) + ke^2/r^2 = 0$, so $r = \hbar^2/(m_eke^2) = a_0$. Substituting back, $E = -m_e(ke^2)^2/(2\hbar^2) = -13.6$ eV. The uncertainty principle alone reproduces the exact ground-state energy here.

name: Bragg reflection of electrons
statement: Electrons accelerated through $200$ V reflect from crystal planes spaced $0.200$ nm apart. At what glancing angle does the first-order Bragg peak ($2d\sin\theta = \lambda$) appear, in degrees? Use $\lambda = 1.226/\sqrt{V}$ nm.
solution: The wavelength is $1.226/\sqrt{200} = 0.0867$ nm. Then $\sin\theta = \lambda/(2d) = 0.0867/0.400 = 0.2167$, so $\theta = 12.5^\circ$.

name: Wavelength equal to particle size
statement: How much kinetic energy must a proton have for its de Broglie wavelength to equal $1.00$ fm, roughly a nucleon diameter? Give the answer in MeV. Use $hc = 1240$ eV$\cdot$nm and $m_pc^2 = 938.3$ MeV, and treat the proton relativistically.
solution: First $pc = hc/\lambda = 1240\ \text{eV}\cdot\text{nm}/10^{-6}\ \text{nm} = 1240$ MeV. Then $E = \sqrt{(1240)^2 + (938.3)^2} = 1555$ MeV, so $K = 1555 - 938 = 617$ MeV. Probing nucleon structure genuinely requires GeV-scale machines.

name: When wavelength meets Compton wavelength
statement: At what kinetic energy does an electron's de Broglie wavelength equal its Compton wavelength $h/(m_ec)$? Give the answer in MeV, using $m_ec^2 = 0.511$ MeV.
solution: Equating $h/p = h/(m_ec)$ gives $p = m_ec$, so $pc = m_ec^2$. Then $E = \sqrt{2}\,m_ec^2$ and $K = (\sqrt{2}-1)(0.511) = 0.212$ MeV. This marks the boundary where relativistic treatment becomes unavoidable.

name: Diffracting a buckyball
statement: C$_{60}$ molecules (mass $720$ u, $1\ \text{u} = 1.6605\times 10^{-27}$ kg) travel at $200$ m/s through a grating in a matter-wave interference experiment. What is their de Broglie wavelength, in pm? Use $h = 6.63\times 10^{-34}$ J$\cdot$s.
solution: The molecular mass is $720(1.6605\times 10^{-27}) = 1.196\times 10^{-24}$ kg, so $p = mv = 2.39\times 10^{-22}$ kg$\cdot$m/s. Then $\lambda = h/p = 2.77\times 10^{-12}$ m $= 2.77$ pm, hundreds of times smaller than the molecule itself, yet still enough to produce clear interference fringes.

name: Decay constant of carbon-14
statement: Carbon-14 has a half-life of $5730$ years. What is its decay constant, in yr$^{-1}$?
solution: The decay constant is $\lambda = \ln 2/T_{1/2}$. So $\lambda = 0.6931/5730 = 1.21\times 10^{-4}$ yr$^{-1}$.

name: Three half-lives
statement: What fraction of a radioactive sample remains after three half-lives have elapsed?
solution: Each half-life halves the amount, so after three the fraction is $(1/2)^3 = 0.125$.

name: Technetium in a hospital
statement: A vial contains $8.00$ g of a tracer with a $6.00$ hour half-life. How much of the tracer remains after $24.0$ hours, in g?
solution: Twenty-four hours is four half-lives, so the remaining fraction is $(1/2)^4 = 1/16$. That leaves $8.00/16 = 0.500$ g.

name: Activity of a sample
statement: A sample contains $1.00\times 10^{20}$ nuclei of an isotope with half-life $10.0$ years. What is its activity, in Bq? Take $1$ yr $= 3.156\times 10^7$ s.
solution: First $\lambda = \ln 2/(10.0 \times 3.156\times 10^7\ \text{s}) = 2.20\times 10^{-9}$ s$^{-1}$. Then $A = \lambda N = 2.20\times 10^{-9} \times 10^{20} = 2.20\times 10^{11}$ Bq.

name: Alpha decay of uranium-238
statement: Uranium-238 ($Z = 92$) emits an alpha particle. What is the mass number of the daughter nucleus?
solution: An alpha particle is $^4_2$He, so the daughter loses 4 from $A$ and 2 from $Z$. The daughter is thorium-234, with $A = 234$.

name: Beta-minus decay of carbon-14
statement: Carbon-14 ($Z = 6$) undergoes $\beta^-$ decay. What is the atomic number of the daughter nucleus?
solution: In $\beta^-$ decay a neutron becomes a proton, an electron, and an antineutrino, so $Z$ rises by one while $A$ is unchanged. The daughter is nitrogen-14 with $Z = 7$.

name: Iodine-131 down to a quarter
statement: Iodine-131 has a half-life of $8.02$ days. How long does it take for a sample's activity to fall to one quarter of its initial value, in days?
solution: One quarter corresponds to two half-lives. So $t = 2(8.02) = 16.0$ days.

name: Half-life from a mean life
statement: The muon has a mean lifetime of $2.20$ $\mu$s. What is its half-life, in $\mu$s?
solution: Mean life and half-life are related by $T_{1/2} = \tau\ln 2$. So $T_{1/2} = 2.20(0.6931) = 1.52$ $\mu$s.

name: Gamma decay bookkeeping
statement: A nucleus in an excited state emits a gamma ray. By how much does its mass number change?
solution: A gamma ray carries away energy and angular momentum but no nucleons and no charge. Both $A$ and $Z$ are unchanged, so the change in $A$ is $0$.

name: Half-life from a Geiger counter
statement: A Geiger counter reads $800$ Bq from a fresh sample and $100$ Bq exactly $30.0$ minutes later. What is the half-life, in minutes?
solution: The activity dropped by a factor of $8 = 2^3$, so three half-lives elapsed. Hence $T_{1/2} = 30.0/3 = 10.0$ minutes.

name: Half-life from two readings
statement: A sample's activity falls from $4.80\times 10^4$ Bq to $1.20\times 10^4$ Bq over $12.0$ days. What is the half-life, in days?
solution: The activity fell by a factor of $4 = 2^2$, which takes two half-lives. So $T_{1/2} = 12.0/2 = 6.00$ days.

name: The curie defined by radium
statement: Radium-226 has a half-life of $1600$ years. What is the activity of exactly $1.00$ g of it, in Bq? Use $N_A = 6.022\times 10^{23}$ and $1$ yr $= 3.156\times 10^7$ s.
solution: One gram contains $N = 6.022\times 10^{23}/226 = 2.66\times 10^{21}$ nuclei, and $\lambda = \ln 2/(1600\times 3.156\times 10^7) = 1.37\times 10^{-11}$ s$^{-1}$. The activity is $A = \lambda N = 3.66\times 10^{10}$ Bq, which is essentially the historical definition of the curie.

name: Radium in uranium ore
statement: In old uranium ore, radium-226 ($T_{1/2} = 1600$ yr) is in secular equilibrium with uranium-238 ($T_{1/2} = 4.468\times 10^9$ yr). What is the ratio of radium nuclei to uranium nuclei?
solution: Secular equilibrium means equal activities, $\lambda_{\rm Ra}N_{\rm Ra} = \lambda_{\rm U}N_{\rm U}$. Hence $N_{\rm Ra}/N_{\rm U} = \lambda_{\rm U}/\lambda_{\rm Ra} = T_{\rm Ra}/T_{\rm U} = 1600/4.468\times 10^9 = 3.58\times 10^{-7}$.

name: Activity at an arbitrary time
statement: A source has activity $5.00\times 10^5$ Bq and half-life $12.7$ hours. What is its activity $30.0$ hours later, in Bq?

name: Counting decays, not rates
statement: A sample starts with $1.00\times 10^{12}$ nuclei of an isotope whose half-life is $1.00$ hour. How many nuclei decay during the first hour?
solution: After one half-life exactly half the nuclei remain, so half have decayed. That is $5.00\times 10^{11}$ decays, not $\lambda N_0 t$, which would overestimate by ignoring the falling population.

name: Becquerels into curies
statement: A medical source has an activity of $250$ MBq. What is this in curies, given $1$ Ci $= 3.70\times 10^{10}$ Bq?
solution: Divide: $2.50\times 10^8/3.70\times 10^{10} = 6.76\times 10^{-3}$ Ci, about $6.8$ mCi.

name: Radon in a sealed basement
statement: A sealed basement starts with a radon-222 concentration of $200$ Bq/m$^3$. Radon-222 has a half-life of $3.82$ days and no new radon enters. What is the concentration after $7.00$ days, in Bq/m$^3$?

name: Branching in potassium-40
statement: Potassium-40 decays $89.3\%$ of the time by $\beta^-$ emission and $10.7\%$ by electron capture. A sample has a total activity of $1000$ Bq. How many electron-capture events occur per second?
solution: Branching ratios split a single total decay rate. The electron-capture rate is $0.107 \times 1000 = 107$ per second.

name: Effective half-life in the body
statement: Iodine-131 has a physical half-life of $8.02$ days, and the thyroid clears it with a biological half-life of $10.0$ days. What is the effective half-life in the body, in days?
solution: Independent removal processes add their rates, so $1/T_{\rm eff} = 1/T_{\rm phys} + 1/T_{\rm bio}$. That gives $1/T_{\rm eff} = 1/8.02 + 1/10.0 = 0.2247$ d$^{-1}$, so $T_{\rm eff} = 4.45$ days.

name: Correcting for detector efficiency
statement: A detector registers $3000$ counts per minute from a source. The detector intercepts and records only $12.0\%$ of the decays. What is the source activity, in Bq?
solution: The true decay rate is $3000/0.120 = 2.50\times 10^4$ per minute. Converting, $A = 2.50\times 10^4/60.0 = 417$ Bq.

name: Radiocarbon age of a campfire
statement: Charcoal from an old campfire gives $0.150$ Bq per gram of carbon, while living wood gives $0.250$ Bq per gram. Carbon-14 has a half-life of $5730$ years. How old is the charcoal, in years?

name: Alpha, beta, gamma stopping
statement: A nucleus decays by emitting, in sequence, one alpha particle and two $\beta^-$ particles. If the original nucleus had $Z = 90$, what is the atomic number of the final nucleus?
solution: Alpha emission lowers $Z$ by $2$; each $\beta^-$ raises $Z$ by $1$. The net change is $-2 + 2 = 0$, so $Z = 90$ again, though $A$ has dropped by $4$.

name: Transient equilibrium in a generator
statement: A technetium generator holds molybdenum-99 ($T_{1/2} = 66.0$ h) decaying to technetium-99m ($T_{1/2} = 6.01$ h). Once transient equilibrium is reached, the activity ratio is $A_d/A_p = \lambda_d/(\lambda_d - \lambda_p)$. What is this ratio? Assume every parent decay feeds the daughter.
solution: The decay constants are $\lambda_d = \ln 2/6.01$ and $\lambda_p = \ln 2/66.0$ per hour. Substituting, $A_d/A_p = (1/6.01)/(1/6.01 - 1/66.0) = 1.10$. The daughter is slightly more active than the parent, and both then decay with the parent's $66$ hour half-life.

name: Uranium-lead dating
statement: A zircon crystal contains $0.300$ lead-206 atoms for every uranium-238 atom, and all the lead came from uranium decay. Uranium-238 has a half-life of $4.468\times 10^9$ years. How old is the crystal, in years?
solution: If $N$ uranium atoms remain and $0.300N$ have decayed, the original number was $1.300N$. Then $t = (T_{1/2}/\ln 2)\ln(1.300) = (6.446\times 10^9)(0.2624) = 1.69\times 10^9$ years.

name: Production and decay in a cyclotron
statement: A cyclotron produces fluorine-18 ($T_{1/2} = 110$ min) at a steady rate of $5.00\times 10^{10}$ nuclei per second. Starting from zero, what is the activity of the target after $120$ minutes of irradiation, in Bq?
solution: With constant production $R$ and decay $\lambda$, the activity grows as $A = R(1 - e^{-\lambda t})$, saturating at $R$. Here $e^{-\lambda t} = 2^{-120/110} = 0.4685$, so $A = 5.00\times 10^{10}(0.5315) = 2.65\times 10^{10}$ Bq.

name: Sharing the alpha decay energy
statement: Polonium-210 alpha decays to lead-206 with $Q = 5.407$ MeV, starting from rest. Using mass numbers for the masses, what kinetic energy does the alpha particle carry, in MeV?
solution: Momentum conservation gives $p_\alpha = p_{\rm Pb}$, so kinetic energies split inversely with mass: $K_\alpha = Q\,m_{\rm Pb}/(m_\alpha + m_{\rm Pb})$. That is $5.407 \times 206/210 = 5.30$ MeV, with the recoiling lead taking the remaining $0.10$ MeV.

name: Absorbed dose from alpha particles
statement: A $70.0$ kg person absorbs $1.00\times 10^{12}$ alpha particles, each of energy $5.00$ MeV. What is the whole-body absorbed dose, in Gy? Use $1\ \text{eV} = 1.602\times 10^{-19}$ J.
solution: Total energy deposited is $10^{12} \times 5.00\times 10^6 \times 1.602\times 10^{-19} = 0.801$ J. Dose is energy per mass: $0.801/70.0 = 0.0114$ Gy.

name: Mixture of two isotopes
statement: A sample contains two isotopes. Isotope A contributes $600$ Bq with half-life $2.00$ h; isotope B contributes $400$ Bq with half-life $20.0$ h. What is the total activity $6.00$ hours later, in Bq?
solution: Each component decays independently, so add the two exponentials rather than using a single half-life. Isotope A falls to $600 \times 2^{-3.00} = 75.0$ Bq and isotope B to $400 \times 2^{-0.300} = 325$ Bq, for a total of $400$ Bq.

name: When is the daughter activity highest?
statement: A freshly purified sample of molybdenum-99 ($T_{1/2} = 66.0$ h) decays to technetium-99m ($T_{1/2} = 6.01$ h), which is initially absent. The Bateman solution peaks at $t = \ln(\lambda_d/\lambda_p)/(\lambda_d - \lambda_p)$. When does the technetium activity reach its maximum, in hours?
solution: The decay constants are $\lambda_p = \ln 2/66.0 = 0.01050$ h$^{-1}$ and $\lambda_d = \ln 2/6.01 = 0.1153$ h$^{-1}$. Then $t = \ln(10.98)/(0.1048) = 2.396/0.1048 = 22.9$ hours. After this the daughter tracks the parent in transient equilibrium.

name: Age of the elements from uranium isotopes
statement: Natural uranium today is $99.28\%$ U-238 ($T_{1/2} = 4.468\times 10^9$ yr) and $0.72\%$ U-235 ($T_{1/2} = 7.04\times 10^8$ yr). Assuming the two isotopes were created in equal numbers, how long ago was that, in years?
solution: The ratio evolves as $N_{235}/N_{238} = e^{-(\lambda_{235}-\lambda_{238})t}$. With $\lambda_{235} = 9.846\times 10^{-10}$ and $\lambda_{238} = 1.551\times 10^{-10}$ per year, $t = \ln(99.28/0.72)/(8.294\times 10^{-10}) = 4.927/8.294\times 10^{-10} = 5.94\times 10^9$ years. Real models start from an r-process ratio nearer $1.6$, but the method is the same.

name: Mass defect of the alpha particle
statement: Helium-4 has atomic mass $4.002603$ u, while $m_H = 1.007825$ u and $m_n = 1.008665$ u. What is the total binding energy of helium-4, in MeV? Use $1$ u $= 931.5$ MeV/c$^2$.
solution: The constituents weigh $2(1.007825) + 2(1.008665) = 4.032980$ u, so the mass defect is $0.030377$ u. Multiplying by $931.5$ gives $28.3$ MeV.

name: Binding energy per nucleon of helium
statement: Helium-4 has a total binding energy of $28.3$ MeV. What is its binding energy per nucleon, in MeV?
solution: Divide by the number of nucleons: $28.3/4 = 7.07$ MeV per nucleon. This is unusually high for such a light nucleus, which is why the alpha particle is so tightly bound.

name: An atomic mass unit in MeV
statement: What is the rest energy equivalent of one atomic mass unit, in MeV?
solution: By definition $1$ u $= 1.6605\times 10^{-27}$ kg, and $E = mc^2$ converts this to $931.5$ MeV. This constant turns every mass difference in u directly into an energy.

name: Binding energy of the deuteron
statement: Deuterium has atomic mass $2.014102$ u, with $m_H = 1.007825$ u and $m_n = 1.008665$ u. What is the binding energy of the deuteron, in MeV? Use $1$ u $= 931.5$ MeV/c$^2$.
solution: The mass defect is $1.007825 + 1.008665 - 2.014102 = 0.002388$ u. Times $931.5$ this is $2.22$ MeV, the weakest binding of any stable nucleus.

name: Energy of one fission
statement: A single uranium-235 fission releases about $200$ MeV. How many joules is that? Use $1\ \text{eV} = 1.602\times 10^{-19}$ J.
solution: Convert directly: $200\times 10^6 \times 1.602\times 10^{-19} = 3.20\times 10^{-11}$ J.

name: Fissions needed for one watt
statement: Each fission releases $3.20\times 10^{-11}$ J. How many fissions per second sustain a power of $1.00$ W?
solution: Divide power by energy per event: $1.00/3.20\times 10^{-11} = 3.12\times 10^{10}$ fissions per second.

name: Rest energy of one kilogram
statement: What is the rest energy of $1.00$ kg of any substance, in J? Use $c = 3.00\times 10^8$ m/s.
solution: $E = mc^2 = 1.00 \times (3.00\times 10^8)^2 = 9.00\times 10^{16}$ J, roughly the yield of a twenty-megaton bomb.

name: Power output of the Sun
statement: The Sun converts $4.30\times 10^9$ kg of mass into energy every second. What is its power output, in W? Use $c = 3.00\times 10^8$ m/s.

name: Binding energy of carbon-12
statement: Carbon-12 has atomic mass exactly $12$ u by definition. Using $m_H = 1.007825$ u and $m_n = 1.008665$ u, what is its total binding energy, in MeV? Use $1$ u $= 931.5$ MeV/c$^2$.
solution: The free constituents weigh $6(1.007825) + 6(1.008665) = 12.098940$ u, so the defect is $0.098940$ u. Multiplying by $931.5$ gives $92.2$ MeV, or $7.68$ MeV per nucleon.

name: Peak of the binding energy curve
statement: The binding energy per nucleon curve peaks near iron-56 at its maximum value. What is that value, in MeV per nucleon? (Give the standard textbook figure to three significant figures: $8.79$.)
solution: Iron-56 and nickel-62 sit at the top of the binding energy curve at about $8.79$ MeV per nucleon. Nuclei lighter than iron release energy by fusing, heavier ones by fissioning, which is why iron is the endpoint of stellar burning.

name: Q value of D-T fusion
statement: Compute the energy released in $^2$H $+$ $^3$H $\to$ $^4$He $+$ n. Atomic masses: $^2$H $= 2.014102$, $^3$H $= 3.016049$, $^4$He $= 4.002603$, n $= 1.008665$ u. Give the answer in MeV, using $1$ u $= 931.5$ MeV/c$^2$.
solution: The reactants total $5.030151$ u and the products $5.011268$ u, a difference of $0.018883$ u. Times $931.5$ this is $17.6$ MeV, the reaction that fusion reactors target because of its large cross section.

name: Q value of D-D fusion
statement: Compute the energy released in $^2$H $+$ $^2$H $\to$ $^3$He $+$ n. Atomic masses: $^2$H $= 2.014102$, $^3$He $= 3.016029$, n $= 1.008665$ u. Give the answer in MeV, using $1$ u $= 931.5$ MeV/c$^2$.
solution: The mass difference is $2(2.014102) - 3.016029 - 1.008665 = 0.003510$ u. Multiplying by $931.5$ gives $3.27$ MeV, considerably less than D-T.

name: Energy of the proton-proton chain
statement: In the Sun, four protons fuse into a helium-4 nucleus with two positrons and two neutrinos. Using atomic masses $m_H = 1.007825$ u and $^4$He $= 4.002603$ u, what total energy is released per helium nucleus, in MeV? Use $1$ u $= 931.5$ MeV/c$^2$.
solution: Working with atomic masses automatically accounts for the two positrons annihilating with two surplus electrons. The defect is $4(1.007825) - 4.002603 = 0.028697$ u, giving $26.7$ MeV, of which the neutrinos carry off a small share.

name: Energy in a kilogram of uranium
statement: Each U-235 fission releases $200$ MeV. How much energy is available in $1.00$ kg of pure U-235, in J? Use $N_A = 6.022\times 10^{23}$ and $1$ MeV $= 1.602\times 10^{-13}$ J.
solution: One kilogram contains $N = (6.022\times 10^{23}/235)(1000) = 2.56\times 10^{24}$ nuclei. Multiplying by $200$ MeV $= 3.204\times 10^{-11}$ J gives $8.21\times 10^{13}$ J, about three million times the energy in a kilogram of coal.

name: Q value of an alpha decay
statement: Polonium-210 ($209.982874$ u) alpha decays to lead-206 ($205.974465$ u), with $^4$He $= 4.002603$ u. What is the Q value, in MeV? Use $1$ u $= 931.5$ MeV/c$^2$.
solution: The mass difference is $209.982874 - 205.974465 - 4.002603 = 0.005806$ u. Times $931.5$ this gives $Q = 5.41$ MeV, shared between the alpha and the recoiling lead.

name: Endpoint of the carbon-14 beta spectrum
statement: Carbon-14 (atomic mass $14.003242$ u) beta decays to nitrogen-14 ($14.003074$ u). What is the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electron, in MeV? Use $1$ u $= 931.5$ MeV/c$^2$.
solution: For $\beta^-$ decay the Q value is the difference in atomic masses, since the extra electron is already included. That is $0.000168$ u $= 0.156$ MeV, which the electron gets when the antineutrino takes nothing.

name: Fission rate in a power reactor
statement: A reactor produces $3000$ MW of thermal power, with $200$ MeV per fission. How many fissions occur per second? Use $1$ MeV $= 1.602\times 10^{-13}$ J.
solution: Each fission delivers $3.204\times 10^{-11}$ J, so the rate is $3.00\times 10^9/3.204\times 10^{-11} = 9.36\times 10^{19}$ fissions per second.

name: Mass consumed by a reactor
statement: A reactor produces $1000$ MW of thermal power. At what rate is rest mass converted to energy, in kg/s? Use $c = 3.00\times 10^8$ m/s.
solution: From $P = \dot{m}c^2$, $\dot{m} = 10^9/(9.00\times 10^{16}) = 1.11\times 10^{-8}$ kg/s. That is about a gram a day, quite separate from the tonnes of fuel consumed.

name: Binding energy of oxygen-16
statement: Oxygen-16 has atomic mass $15.994915$ u. Using $m_H = 1.007825$ u and $m_n = 1.008665$ u, what is its binding energy per nucleon, in MeV? Use $1$ u $= 931.5$ MeV/c$^2$.
solution: The constituents weigh $8(1.007825) + 8(1.008665) = 16.131920$ u, so the defect is $0.137005$ u $= 127.6$ MeV. Dividing by $16$ gives $7.98$ MeV per nucleon.

name: Photodisintegration of the deuteron
statement: What minimum photon energy can split a deuteron into a free proton and neutron? Ignore nuclear recoil. Give the answer in MeV.
solution: The photon must supply the full binding energy of the deuteron, $2.22$ MeV. Including recoil raises the true threshold by only about $1$ keV.

name: Fusion versus fission per nucleon
statement: D-T fusion releases $17.6$ MeV from $5$ nucleons. What is the energy released per nucleon, in MeV?
solution: Divide: $17.6/5 = 3.52$ MeV per nucleon. Fission of U-235 gives only $200/236 = 0.85$ MeV per nucleon, so fusion is roughly four times more energetic per unit mass.

name: Neutron separation energy
statement: Helium-4 has binding energy $28.3$ MeV and helium-3 has binding energy $7.72$ MeV. How much energy is needed to remove one neutron from helium-4, in MeV?
solution: The separation energy is the difference in total binding energies: $S_n = B(^4\text{He}) - B(^3\text{He}) = 28.3 - 7.72 = 20.6$ MeV. This large gap is why helium-4 is so hard to break up.

name: Semi-empirical mass formula for calcium-40
statement: Use the semi-empirical mass formula $$B = a_vA - a_sA^{2/3} - a_c\frac{Z(Z-1)}{A^{1/3}} - a_{\rm sym}\frac{(A-2Z)^2}{A} + \frac{12}{\sqrt{A}}$$ with $a_v = 15.75$, $a_s = 17.8$, $a_c = 0.711$, $a_{\rm sym} = 23.7$ MeV (the last term applies since calcium-40 is even-even). What binding energy does it predict for $^{40}$Ca, in MeV?
solution: Term by term: volume $+630.0$, surface $-208.2$, Coulomb $-0.711(20)(19)/3.420 = -79.0$, asymmetry $0$ since $N = Z$, pairing $+1.90$. The sum is $345$ MeV, close to the measured $342$ MeV.

name: Coulomb barrier for two deuterons
statement: Two deuterons must approach within $3.00$ fm to fuse. Using $ke^2 = 1.44$ MeV$\cdot$fm, what is the height of the Coulomb barrier, in MeV?
solution: The electrostatic energy of two unit charges at separation $r$ is $ke^2/r = 1.44/3.00 = 0.480$ MeV. A thermal plasma would need billions of kelvin to clear this classically, which is why tunneling matters so much in stars.

name: Fuel burn rate of a fusion plant
statement: A fusion plant delivers $1.00$ GW of electricity at $40.0\%$ thermal efficiency, burning D-T at $17.6$ MeV per reaction. How many kilograms of deuterium plus tritium does it consume per day? Use $1$ MeV $= 1.602\times 10^{-13}$ J, $1$ u $= 1.6605\times 10^{-27}$ kg, and $5.030$ u per reaction.
solution: The thermal power is $2.50$ GW, and each reaction gives $2.82\times 10^{-12}$ J, so the rate is $8.87\times 10^{20}$ reactions per second. Each consumes $5.030$ u $= 8.35\times 10^{-27}$ kg, giving $7.41\times 10^{-6}$ kg/s, or $0.640$ kg per day.

name: Binding energy per nucleon of uranium
statement: Uranium-238 has atomic mass $238.050788$ u. Using $m_H = 1.007825$ u and $m_n = 1.008665$ u, what is its binding energy per nucleon, in MeV? Use $1$ u $= 931.5$ MeV/c$^2$.
solution: The $92$ hydrogen atoms and $146$ neutrons weigh $239.98499$ u, so the defect is $1.934202$ u $= 1801.7$ MeV. Dividing by $238$ gives $7.57$ MeV per nucleon, well below iron's peak, which is exactly why uranium can fission and release energy.

name: Fusing helium into oxygen
statement: Four alpha particles fuse into one oxygen-16 nucleus. Helium-4 has binding energy $28.3$ MeV and oxygen-16 has $127.6$ MeV. How much energy is released, in MeV?
solution: Energy released equals the gain in total binding energy: $127.6 - 4(28.3) = 127.6 - 113.2 = 14.4$ MeV. The gain is modest because alpha particles are already tightly bound, which is why helium burning yields far less per nucleon than hydrogen burning.

name: Is spontaneous fission energetically allowed?
statement: Uranium-238 has $7.57$ MeV per nucleon of binding energy. Suppose it split into two identical palladium-119 fragments with $8.50$ MeV per nucleon. How much energy would this release, in MeV?
solution: Compare total binding energies: before, $238(7.57) = 1802$ MeV; after, $238(8.50) = 2023$ MeV. The release is the increase, $2023 - 1802 = 221$ MeV. Spontaneous fission is therefore hugely exothermic, and only the Coulomb barrier makes U-238 essentially stable.

name: Most stable charge for a given mass number
statement: Maximizing the semi-empirical binding energy over $Z$ at fixed $A$ gives $$Z_{\min} = \frac{A}{2 + (a_c/2a_{\rm sym})A^{2/3}}.$$ With $a_c = 0.711$ MeV and $a_{\rm sym} = 23.7$ MeV, what value does this predict for $A = 125$?
solution: Here $a_c/(2a_{\rm sym}) = 0.711/47.4 = 0.0150$ and $A^{2/3} = 25.0$, so the denominator is $2 + 0.375 = 2.375$. Then $Z_{\min} = 125/2.375 = 52.6$, and indeed the stable $A = 125$ nuclide is tellurium-125 with $Z = 52$.

name: Lifetime of the Sun's hydrogen
statement: The Sun's core holds about $10\%$ of its $2.0\times 10^{30}$ kg as hydrogen available for fusion. Hydrogen burning converts $0.71\%$ of the fuel's rest mass into energy, and the Sun radiates $3.9\times 10^{26}$ W. For how many years can it sustain this? Use $c = 3.00\times 10^8$ m/s and $1$ yr $= 3.16\times 10^7$ s.
solution: The available fuel is $2.0\times 10^{29}$ kg, of which $0.71\%$, or $1.42\times 10^{27}$ kg, becomes energy: $E = mc^2 = 1.28\times 10^{44}$ J. Dividing by the luminosity gives $3.28\times 10^{17}$ s, which is $1.0\times 10^{10}$ years.

name: Baryon number of the proton
statement: What is the baryon number of a proton?
solution: Each quark carries baryon number $1/3$, and the proton is $uud$. The total is $3 \times 1/3 = 1$.

name: Charge of the up quark
statement: What is the electric charge of an up quark, in units of the elementary charge $e$?
solution: Up-type quarks ($u$, $c$, $t$) carry charge $+2/3$, and down-type quarks carry $-1/3$. So the answer is $+2/3 = 0.667$.

name: Charge of the neutron from its quarks
statement: The neutron has quark content $udd$. What is its total electric charge, in units of $e$?
solution: Summing charges, $+2/3 - 1/3 - 1/3 = 0$. The neutron is electrically neutral despite being made of charged constituents.

name: Lepton number of a neutrino
statement: What is the electron lepton number of an electron neutrino $\nu_e$?
solution: Electrons and electron neutrinos both carry $L_e = +1$; their antiparticles carry $-1$. So $\nu_e$ has $L_e = +1$.

name: Quarks in a baryon
statement: How many valence quarks does a baryon contain?
solution: By definition a baryon is a colour-singlet built from three valence quarks, giving baryon number $1$. Mesons, by contrast, contain a quark and an antiquark.

name: Strangeness of the lambda
statement: The $\Lambda^0$ baryon has quark content $uds$. What is its strangeness?
solution: By convention the strange quark carries strangeness $-1$ and the antistrange $+1$. With one $s$ quark, the $\Lambda^0$ has $S = -1$.

name: Photons from a neutral pion
statement: A $\pi^0$ of rest energy $135$ MeV decays at rest into two photons. What is the energy of each photon, in MeV?
solution: Momentum conservation makes the two photons back-to-back with equal energies, and energy conservation splits the rest energy evenly. Each photon carries $135/2 = 67.5$ MeV.

name: Charge of the omega-minus
statement: The $\Omega^-$ baryon has quark content $sss$. What is its charge, in units of $e$?
solution: Each strange quark has charge $-1/3$, so three of them give $-1$. Its predicted existence and properties were a famous early success of the quark model.

name: Quark generations
statement: How many generations of quarks does the Standard Model contain?
solution: The quarks come in three generations: $(u,d)$, $(c,s)$, and $(t,b)$, so six flavours in all. The leptons are organized the same way.

name: Annihilation photon energy
statement: An electron and a positron annihilate at rest into two photons. What is the energy of each photon, in MeV? Use $m_ec^2 = 0.511$ MeV.
solution: The total rest energy is $2(0.511) = 1.022$ MeV, split equally between two back-to-back photons. Each carries $0.511$ MeV, the signature line of PET imaging.

name: Why the proton is stable
statement: The decay $p \to e^+ + \gamma$ is never observed. What is the magnitude of the change in baryon number that this decay would require?
solution: The proton has $B = 1$ while the positron and photon both have $B = 0$. The decay would change $B$ by $1$, and baryon number conservation is what keeps the proton stable.

name: Counting allowed decays
statement:
Consider these five processes: (i) $n 	o p + e^- +  ar{
u}_e$, (ii) $\mu^- 	o e^- + \gamma$, (iii) $\pi^+ 	o \mu^+ + 
u_\mu$, (iv) $p 	o n + e^+ + 
u_e$ for a free proton, (v) $\Lambda^0 	o p + \pi^-$. How many are allowed by both the conservation laws and energy conservation?
solution: Process (i) conserves charge, baryon number and lepton number and is exothermic. Process (ii) violates separate muon and electron lepton numbers. Process (iv) is forbidden because a free proton is lighter than a neutron. Processes (iii) and (v) are ordinary weak decays, so three are allowed.

name: Strangeness in a weak decay
statement: In the decay $\Lambda^0 \to p + \pi^-$, what is the change in strangeness, $S_{\rm final} - S_{\rm initial}$?
solution: The $\Lambda^0$ has $S = -1$, while the proton and pion both have $S = 0$. So $\Delta S = +1$, which is allowed only for the weak interaction and explains the $\Lambda$'s long lifetime.

name: Antiproton threshold on a fixed target
statement: Antiprotons are made in $p + p \to p + p + p + \bar{p}$ using a beam on a stationary hydrogen target. What is the minimum beam kinetic energy, in GeV? Use $m_pc^2 = 0.9383$ GeV.
solution: Using invariants with all four particles at rest in the CM frame, $s = (4m_p)^2c^4$ gives $K_{\rm th} = 6m_pc^2$. Numerically $6(0.9383) = 5.63$ GeV, which set the design energy of the Bevatron.

name: Identifying a missing particle
statement: In the reaction $p + p \to p + n + X$, what is the electric charge of $X$, in units of $e$?
solution: Charge must balance: the initial state has $+2$, the visible products have $+1$. So $X$ carries $+1$, and since baryon number is already accounted for, $X$ is a $\pi^+$.

name: Lepton numbers in muon decay
statement: In $\mu^- \to e^- + \bar{\nu}_e + \nu_\mu$, what is the total muon lepton number $L_\mu$ of the final state?
solution: Only the $\nu_\mu$ carries muon number, and it has $L_\mu = +1$. This matches the initial $\mu^-$, so $L_\mu$ is conserved; the $e^-$ and $\bar{\nu}_e$ pair likewise gives $L_e = 0$.

name: Lifetime from a resonance width
statement: The $\rho$ meson appears as a resonance $150$ MeV wide. What is its lifetime, in s? Use $\hbar = 6.582\times 10^{-22}$ MeV$\cdot$s.
solution: The width and lifetime satisfy $\Gamma\tau = \hbar$. So $\tau = 6.582\times 10^{-22}/150 = 4.39\times 10^{-24}$ s, characteristic of a strong decay.

name: Quarks in a meson
statement: How many valence quarks and antiquarks does a meson contain in total?
solution: A meson is a quark-antiquark pair, so two valence constituents in all, giving baryon number $1/3 - 1/3 = 0$.

name: Strangeness of the negative kaon
statement: The $K^-$ meson has quark content $s\bar{u}$. What is its strangeness?
solution: The $s$ quark carries $S = -1$ and the $\bar{u}$ carries none, so $S(K^-) = -1$. Its antiparticle $K^+ = \bar{s}u$ has $S = +1$.

name: Collider centre-of-mass energy
statement: Two proton beams of $6.50$ TeV each collide head-on. What is the centre-of-mass energy, in TeV?
solution: In a symmetric collider the lab frame is already the CM frame, so the energies simply add: $\sqrt{s} = 2(6.50) = 13.0$ TeV.

name: Charge of the sigma-plus
statement: The $\Sigma^+$ has quark content $uus$. What is its charge, in units of $e$?
solution: Adding charges, $2/3 + 2/3 - 1/3 = +1$. Its strangeness is $-1$, so it decays weakly with a lifetime of about $10^{-10}$ s.

name: Counting fundamental fermions
statement: Counting quark flavours and lepton flavours but ignoring colour and antiparticles, how many fundamental fermions does the Standard Model contain?
solution: There are six quark flavours ($u,d,c,s,t,b$) and six leptons ($e,\mu,\tau$ and their neutrinos), giving $12$. Including three colours for each quark would raise the count to $24$.

name: Fixed target versus collider
statement: A $7.00$ TeV proton beam strikes a stationary hydrogen target. At these energies $\sqrt{s} \approx \sqrt{2m_pc^2E}$. What centre-of-mass energy is available, in GeV? Use $m_pc^2 = 0.9383$ GeV.
solution: Substituting, $\sqrt{s} = \sqrt{2(0.9383)(7000)} = \sqrt{1.314\times 10^4} = 115$ GeV. A collider with the same beam energy delivers $14$ TeV, over a hundred times more, which is why fixed-target machines were abandoned at the high-energy frontier.

name: Photoproduction threshold for a pion
statement: A photon strikes a proton at rest to make $\gamma + p \to p + \pi^0$. Using $m_pc^2 = 938.3$ MeV and $m_\pi c^2 = 135.0$ MeV, what is the threshold photon energy, in MeV?
solution: At threshold the products move together, so $s = (m_p+m_\pi)^2c^4$. Expanding $s = m_p^2c^4 + 2m_pc^2E_\gamma$ gives $E_\gamma = m_\pi c^2(2m_pc^2+m_\pi c^2)/(2m_pc^2) = 135(2011.6)/1876.6 = 145$ MeV.

name: Momentum in a lambda decay
statement: A $\Lambda^0$ ($1115.7$ MeV/c$^2$) at rest decays to a proton ($938.3$) and a $\pi^-$ ($139.6$). What is the momentum of each product, in MeV/c? Use $$p = \frac{\sqrt{[M^2-(m_1+m_2)^2][M^2-(m_1-m_2)^2]}}{2M}c.$$
solution: The two products leave back-to-back with equal momentum magnitudes. Substituting, $M^2 - (m_1+m_2)^2 = 1.2448\times 10^6 - 1.1622\times 10^6$ and $M^2 - (m_1-m_2)^2 = 1.2448\times 10^6 - 6.383\times 10^5$, giving $p = 101$ MeV/c.

name: How many conservation laws are broken?
statement: Consider the proposed reaction $p + \pi^- \to K^+ + \pi^-$. Counting electric charge, baryon number, and strangeness, how many of these three quantities are not conserved?
solution: Charge: $+1-1 = 0$ before and $+1-1 = 0$ after, so charge is fine. Baryon number goes from $1$ to $0$, and strangeness from $0$ to $+1$. Two of the three are violated, so the reaction cannot occur.

name: Flight distance of a kaon
statement: A $K^0_S$ (mass $497.6$ MeV/c$^2$, proper lifetime $0.895\times 10^{-10}$ s) is produced with momentum $5.00$ GeV/c. What is its mean decay length in the lab, in m? Use $c = 3.00\times 10^8$ m/s.
solution: The lab decay length is $L = \gamma\beta c\tau$, and conveniently $\gamma\beta = pc/mc^2 = 5000/497.6 = 10.05$. Then $L = 10.05(3.00\times 10^8)(0.895\times 10^{-10}) = 0.270$ m, so the decay vertex is resolvable in a detector.

name: Charm from the quark model
statement: The $\Lambda_c^+$ baryon has quark content $udc$, where the charm quark has charge $+2/3$. What is its charge, in units of $e$?
solution: Summing $2/3 - 1/3 + 2/3 = +1$. Replacing the $s$ in the $\Lambda^0$ by a $c$ raises the charge by one unit, since $c$ is an up-type quark and $s$ a down-type.

name: The GZK cutoff
statement: An ultra-high-energy proton collides head-on with a cosmic microwave background photon of energy $6.60\times 10^{-4}$ eV, making a $\Delta^+$ resonance of mass $1232$ MeV/c$^2$. The threshold condition is $E_p = [(m_\Delta c^2)^2 - (m_pc^2)^2]/(4E_\gamma)$. What proton energy does this require, in eV? Use $m_pc^2 = 938.3$ MeV.
solution: The numerator is $(1232)^2 - (938.3)^2 = 6.374\times 10^5$ MeV$^2$, which is $6.374\times 10^{17}$ eV$^2$. Dividing by $4E_\gamma = 2.64\times 10^{-3}$ eV gives $2.41\times 10^{20}$ eV, the GZK cutoff above which the universe is opaque to cosmic-ray protons.

name: Photon from a sigma-zero decay
statement: A $\Sigma^0$ ($1192.6$ MeV/c$^2$) at rest decays electromagnetically to a $\Lambda^0$ ($1115.7$ MeV/c$^2$) and a photon. What is the photon energy, in MeV?
solution: Conserving energy and momentum with a massless photon gives $E_\gamma = (M^2 - m^2)c^2/(2M)$. Here $E_\gamma = (1.4223\times 10^6 - 1.2448\times 10^6)/(2385.2) = 74.4$ MeV, slightly less than the $76.9$ MeV mass difference because the $\Lambda$ recoils.

name: Uncertainty in a sum of two lengths
statement: Two rods are measured separately: $L_1 = 2.50 \pm 0.03$ m and $L_2 = 1.20 \pm 0.04$ m. They are laid end to end. What is the uncertainty in the total length, in m?
solution: Independent uncertainties add in quadrature for a sum: $\delta L = \sqrt{\delta L_1^2 + \delta L_2^2}$. So $\delta L = \sqrt{0.03^2 + 0.04^2} = \sqrt{0.0025} = 0.050$ m. The absolute uncertainties combine, not the fractional ones.

name: Fractional uncertainty in an area
statement: A rectangular plate measures $a = 12.0 \pm 0.2$ cm by $b = 8.0 \pm 0.3$ cm. What is the percent uncertainty in its area, in percent?
solution: For a product, fractional uncertainties add in quadrature: $\frac{\delta A}{A} = \sqrt{(\delta a/a)^2 + (\delta b/b)^2}$. Here $\delta a/a = 0.01667$ and $\delta b/b = 0.03750$, giving $\sqrt{2.78\times10^{-4} + 1.406\times10^{-3}} = 0.0410$. The area is uncertain by 4.10 percent, dominated by the shorter side.

name: Standard error of five timings
statement: A stopwatch is used five times to time the same process, giving 10.1, 10.3, 9.8, 10.2, 10.0 s. What is the standard error of the mean, in s?
solution: The mean is 10.08 s. The sample standard deviation uses $N-1$ in the denominator: $s = \sqrt{0.148/4} = 0.192$ s. The standard error is $s/\sqrt{N} = 0.192/\sqrt{5} = 0.086$ s.

name: Slope from two points on a graph
statement: A straight line on a graph of velocity (m/s) against time (s) passes through the points $(2.0,\ 5.0)$ and $(8.0,\ 17.0)$. What is the slope, in m/s^2?
solution: The slope is the rise over the run: $(17.0-5.0)/(8.0-2.0) = 12.0/6.0 = 2.00$ m/s$^2$. Use widely separated points on the drawn line, not raw data points, to reduce reading error.

name: Power-law exponent from a log-log plot
statement: The drag force on a sphere is modeled as $F = k v^{n}$. Two measurements give $F = 0.80$ N at $v = 2.0$ m/s and $F = 6.5$ N at $v = 6.0$ m/s. What is $n$, unitless?
solution: On a log-log plot the exponent is the slope: $n = \frac{\ln(F_2/F_1)}{\ln(v_2/v_1)}$. Here $n = \ln(8.125)/\ln(3.0) = 2.095/1.0986 = 1.91$. The result sits between the linear and quadratic drag laws.

name: Weighted average of two measurements of g
statement: Two independent experiments give $g = 9.79 \pm 0.03$ m/s^2 and $g = 9.83 \pm 0.02$ m/s^2. What is the weighted average, in m/s^2?
solution: Weight each result by $1/\sigma_i^2$: $w_1 = 1111$ and $w_2 = 2500$. Then $\bar{g} = \frac{\sum w_i g_i}{\sum w_i} = \frac{9.79(1111)+9.83(2500)}{3611} = 9.818$ m/s$^2$. The more precise measurement pulls the average toward itself.

name: Uncertainty of a weighted average
statement: For the two results $g = 9.79 \pm 0.03$ m/s^2 and $g = 9.83 \pm 0.02$ m/s^2, what is the uncertainty of the weighted average, in m/s^2?
solution: The variance of a weighted mean is $\sigma^2 = 1/\sum w_i$ with $w_i = 1/\sigma_i^2$. Here $\sum w_i = 1111 + 2500 = 3611$, so $\sigma = 1/\sqrt{3611} = 0.0166$ m/s$^2$. Note this is smaller than either individual uncertainty.

name: Spring constant from a linearized plot
statement: For a mass on a spring, $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$. A student plots $T^2$ against $m$ and obtains a straight line of slope $3.95$ s^2/kg through the origin. What is $k$, in N/m?
solution: Squaring gives $T^2 = \frac{4\pi^2}{k}m$, so the slope is $4\pi^2/k$. Therefore $k = 4\pi^2/3.95 = 39.48/3.95 = 9.99$ N/m. Plotting $T^2$ rather than $T$ is what makes the relation linear.

name: Least-squares slope from a short table
statement:
A student records the following pairs.
x = 1.0, y = 2.1
x = 2.0, y = 3.9
x = 3.0, y = 6.2
x = 4.0, y = 7.9
x = 5.0, y = 10.1
What is the least-squares slope of the best-fit line $y = mx + b$, unitless?
solution: Use $m = \frac{\sum(x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})}{\sum(x_i-\bar{x})^2}$ with $\bar{x}=3.00$ and $\bar{y}=6.04$. The numerator is $20.0$ and the denominator is $10.0$, so $m = 2.00$.

name: Intercept of the same fit
statement: For the data of the previous problem (means $\bar{x} = 3.00$, $\bar{y} = 6.04$, least-squares slope $m = 2.00$), what is the intercept $b$, unitless?
solution: The least-squares line passes through the centroid $(\bar{x},\bar{y})$, so $b = \bar{y} - m\bar{x}$. This gives $b = 6.04 - 2.00(3.00) = 0.04$. The intercept is consistent with zero at this precision.

name: Uncertainty in a density
statement: A sphere has mass $m = 45.2 \pm 0.3$ g and radius $r = 2.20 \pm 0.02$ cm. Its density is $\rho = m/(\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3)$. What is the percent uncertainty in $\rho$, in percent?
solution: For $\rho \propto m r^{-3}$, $\frac{\delta\rho}{\rho} = \sqrt{(\delta m/m)^2 + (3\delta r/r)^2}$. With $\delta m/m = 0.00664$ and $3\delta r/r = 0.0273$, the total is $\sqrt{4.41\times10^{-5}+7.44\times10^{-4}} = 0.0281$, i.e. 2.81 percent. The cube makes the radius dominate even though it is measured to better than 1 percent.

name: Choosing what to plot for constant acceleration
statement: A cart accelerates uniformly along a straight track, and its speed is measured at several positions. A student plots $v^2$ against $x$ and gets a straight line of slope $7.30$ m/s^2 per m. What is the acceleration, in m/s^2?
solution: From $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2ax$, a plot of $v^2$ versus $x$ is linear with slope $2a$ and intercept $v_0^2$. Hence $a = 7.30/2 = 3.65$ m/s$^2$. Plotting $v$ against $x$ would have given a curve and no simple slope.

name: Reading a prefactor off a log-log plot
statement: A power law $y = A x^{n}$ is plotted as $\log_{10} y$ against $\log_{10} x$. The line passes through $(\log_{10}x, \log_{10}y) = (0.50,\ 1.20)$ and $(2.00,\ 3.00)$. What is $A$, unitless?
solution: The slope gives $n = (3.00-1.20)/(2.00-0.50) = 1.20$, and the intercept at $\log_{10}x = 0$ is $\log_{10}A = 1.20 - 1.20(0.50) = 0.60$. So $A = 10^{0.60} = 3.98$. Reading $A$ requires extrapolating to $x = 1$, not just measuring the slope.

name: Uncertainty in a small difference
statement: Two times are measured as $t_1 = 12.48 \pm 0.05$ s and $t_2 = 12.31 \pm 0.05$ s. What is the percent uncertainty in the difference $\Delta t = t_1 - t_2$, in percent?
solution: The absolute uncertainty of a difference is $\sqrt{0.05^2+0.05^2} = 0.0707$ s, while $\Delta t = 0.17$ s. The fractional uncertainty is $0.0707/0.17 = 0.416$, i.e. 41.6 percent. Subtracting nearly equal numbers destroys precision, which is why one should measure $\Delta t$ directly when possible.

name: Significant figures in a quotient
statement: A resistor carries $I = 0.035$ A under a potential difference $V = 12.0$ V. Report $R = V/I$ with the correct number of significant figures. What value do you report, in ohm?
solution: The quotient is $12.0/0.035 = 342.857$ ohm, but the current has only two significant figures, so the result is limited to two. Rounding gives $R = 3.4\times10^{2}$ ohm, i.e. 340 ohm. Writing 342.9 ohm would claim precision the current measurement does not support.

name: Counting statistics
statement: A detector records 2500 decays in a fixed interval. Radioactive counts follow Poisson statistics, so the uncertainty in $N$ counts is $\sqrt{N}$. What is the percent uncertainty in the count rate, in percent?
solution: The uncertainty is $\sqrt{2500} = 50$ counts. The fractional uncertainty is $50/2500 = 0.020$, i.e. 2.00 percent. Note that $\delta N/N = 1/\sqrt{N}$, so quadrupling the counting time halves the percent uncertainty.

name: Best-fit line forced through the origin
statement:
Theory says $y$ is strictly proportional to $x$, so the fit must pass through the origin. The data are
x = 2.0, y = 3.1
x = 4.0, y = 6.3
x = 6.0, y = 9.0
x = 8.0, y = 12.4
What is the least-squares slope, unitless?
solution: Minimizing $\sum (y_i - mx_i)^2$ with no intercept gives $m = \frac{\sum x_i y_i}{\sum x_i^2}$. Here $\sum x_iy_i = 184.6$ and $\sum x_i^2 = 120$, so $m = 1.54$. This differs from the unconstrained fit because the origin is treated as an exact data point.

name: Uncertainty of a least-squares slope
statement:
For the five points
x = 1.0, y = 2.1
x = 2.0, y = 3.9
x = 3.0, y = 6.2
x = 4.0, y = 7.9
x = 5.0, y = 10.1
the best fit is $y = 2.00x + 0.04$. Using $\sigma_m^2 = \frac{1}{N-2}\frac{\sum r_i^2}{\sum (x_i-\bar{x})^2}$ with $r_i$ the residuals, what is the uncertainty in the slope, unitless?
solution: The residuals are $+0.06, -0.14, +0.16, -0.14, +0.06$, so $\sum r_i^2 = 0.072$. With $N-2 = 3$ and $\sum(x_i-\bar{x})^2 = 10.0$, $\sigma_m^2 = (0.072/3)/10.0 = 2.4\times10^{-3}$, giving $\sigma_m = 0.049$. Spreading the $x$ values further apart is the cheapest way to shrink this.

name: Uncertainty in a fitted exponent
statement: A power law $y = Ax^n$ is probed at two values of $x$ that differ by a factor of exactly 10. Each $y$ measurement carries a 2.0 percent uncertainty and the $x$ values are exact. What is the resulting uncertainty in $n$, unitless?
solution: Since $n = \frac{\ln y_2 - \ln y_1}{\ln(x_2/x_1)}$ and $\delta(\ln y) = \delta y/y$, the numerator has uncertainty $\sqrt{2}(0.020) = 0.0283$. Dividing by $\ln 10 = 2.303$ gives $\delta n = 0.0123$. A wider lever arm in $x$ directly buys a better exponent.

name: Error in g from a pendulum timing
statement: A pendulum of length $L = 1.000 \pm 0.005$ m is timed over 20 full oscillations: $20T = 40.12 \pm 0.20$ s. Using $g = 4\pi^2 L/T^2$, what is the uncertainty in $g$, in m/s^2?
solution: Here $T = 2.006$ s and $\delta T = 0.010$ s, giving $g = 4\pi^2(1.000)/2.006^2 = 9.81$ m/s$^2$. Since $g \propto L T^{-2}$, $\frac{\delta g}{g} = \sqrt{(\delta L/L)^2 + (2\delta T/T)^2} = \sqrt{(0.0050)^2+(0.00997)^2} = 0.01115$. Hence $\delta g = 0.109$ m/s$^2$; timing many oscillations at once is what keeps the period term from dominating even more.

name: Error budget for Young's modulus
statement: A wire experiment gives $Y = \frac{4FL}{\pi d^2 e}$. The fractional uncertainties are 1.0 percent in $F$, 0.5 percent in $L$, 1.5 percent in the diameter $d$, and 3.0 percent in the extension $e$. What is the percent uncertainty in $Y$, in percent?
solution: Each factor contributes its fractional uncertainty times the magnitude of its exponent, added in quadrature: $\sqrt{1.0^2 + 0.5^2 + (2\times1.5)^2 + 3.0^2} = \sqrt{19.25} = 4.39$ percent. The diameter matters as much as the extension despite being measured three times better, because it enters squared.

name: Required timing precision
statement: You want $g$ from $g = 4\pi^2L/T^2$ to 0.10 percent. The length is already known to 0.050 percent. What is the largest fractional uncertainty in the period you can tolerate, in percent?
solution: The budget is $(\delta g/g)^2 = (\delta L/L)^2 + (2\delta T/T)^2$, so $(2\delta T/T)^2 = (0.0010)^2-(0.00050)^2 = 7.5\times10^{-7}$. Then $2\delta T/T = 8.66\times10^{-4}$ and $\delta T/T = 4.33\times10^{-4}$, i.e. 0.0433 percent. Timing 100 swings instead of one is the standard way to reach this.

name: Time constant from a semilog fit
statement:
An oscillation amplitude decays as $A = A_0 e^{-t/\tau}$. Measurements:
t = 0 s, A = 100 mm
t = 10 s, A = 74 mm
t = 20 s, A = 55 mm
t = 30 s, A = 41 mm
Fit $\ln A$ against $t$ by least squares. What is $\tau$, in s?
solution: Taking logs linearizes the decay: $\ln A = \ln A_0 - t/\tau$, so the slope is $-1/\tau$. The logs are 4.6052, 4.3041, 4.0073, 3.7136 with mean 4.1575; with $\bar{t} = 15$ s, $\sum(t-\bar{t})(\ln A - \overline{\ln A}) = -14.86$ and $\sum(t-\bar{t})^2 = 500$, so the slope is $-0.02972$ s$^{-1}$. Hence $\tau = 33.7$ s.

name: Half-life from the same fit
statement: Using the fitted decay constant $1/\tau = 0.02972$ s^-1 from the previous fit, what is the time for the amplitude to fall to half its value, in s?
solution: Setting $e^{-t/\tau} = 1/2$ gives $t_{1/2} = \tau \ln 2$. With $1/\tau = 0.02972$ s$^{-1}$, $t_{1/2} = 0.6931/0.02972 = 23.3$ s. This is shorter than $\tau$ by the factor $\ln 2$.

name: Weighted average of three results
statement: Three groups report $g = 9.78 \pm 0.05$, $9.82 \pm 0.03$, and $9.80 \pm 0.02$ m/s^2. What is the weighted average, in m/s^2?
solution: The weights $1/\sigma_i^2$ are 400, 1111, and 2500, summing to 4011. The weighted mean is $\frac{9.78(400)+9.82(1111)+9.80(2500)}{4011} = 9.804$ m/s$^2$. The least precise result contributes only 10 percent of the total weight.

name: Are two results consistent?
statement: Two labs report $g = 9.81 \pm 0.03$ m/s^2 and $g = 9.74 \pm 0.04$ m/s^2. By how many combined standard deviations do the results differ, unitless?
